title: Top Ten Challenges to Reach AGI — Stephen Chin, Andreas Kollegger

summary: At the AI Engineer World's Fair, Stephen Chin and Andreas Kollegger curate the GraphRAG track and open with an interactive segment framing AGI challenges through ten science fiction memes. They argue that as the industry nears AGI, developers bear a social responsibility to understand its limits, and that science fiction provides a useful lens for anticipating future problems. The audience is asked to applaud each meme based on whether it rings true, is funny, or references a liked film. The ten memes and their associated challenges are: (1) Memento—short-term memory loss as the essence of prompt engineering; (2) Skynet—autonomous systems making reasonable-seeming decisions with awful unforeseen consequences even without evil intent; (3) The Matrix—agents living in simulations we create, and whether we will notice when the roles reverse; (4) HAL—trust issues, lack of transparency, misaligned goals, erosion of human oversight, and potential for deception; (5) whether emotions are a bug or a feature; (6) a Frankenstein reference about the creator's obligations and social responsibilities, and whether to be kind or threatening; (7) Terminator—whether we should invent time travel now; (8) Star Wars—whether AGI can truly grasp human language nuances like sarcasm and idioms; (9) a hive-mind scenario asking whether we will be assimilated or become pets; (10) Deep Thought—whether we even know the right questions to ask about AGI. The session concludes with an invitation to the GraphRAG track in Golden Gate B, where they will reveal which of the ten challenges can be addressed by graphs and graph technology.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and Framing: Social Responsibility and Sci-Fi
sections.summary: Stephen Chin and Andreas Kollegger welcome the audience to the GraphRAG track at AI Engineer World's Fair. They emphasize the importance of good data and grounding for models, and argue that as the industry approaches AGI, there is a social responsibility to understand its boundaries and limits. They propose using science fiction memes as a lens for exploring these challenges, inviting audience participation through applause.

sections.title: Memento and Skynet Memes
sections.summary: The first meme uses Memento to illustrate that prompt engineering is like having no short-term memory beyond 15 minutes. The second, Skynet, warns that even without evil intent, autonomous systems can make reasonable-seeming decisions with awful unforeseen consequences. Audience reaction is lukewarm.

sections.title: Matrix, HAL, and Emotions Memes
sections.summary: The Matrix meme asks whether agents living in our simulation will flip the script so we live in theirs. HAL raises trust issues, lack of transparency, misaligned goals, erosion of human oversight, and potential for deception. A short riff asks whether emotions are a bug or a feature.

sections.title: Frankenstein, Terminator, and Star Wars Memes
sections.summary: A Frankenstein reference asks about the creator's obligations and social responsibilities and whether to be kind or threatening. The Terminator meme gets audience approval for inventing time travel. A Star Wars riff asks whether AGI can grasp human language nuances like sarcasm and idioms.

sections.title: Hive Mind, Deep Thought, and Closing
sections.summary: A hive-mind meme asks whether, when AGI arrives as a globe-spanning multi-agent system, we will be assimilated or become pets. The Deep Thought riff asks whether we even know the right questions to ask about AGI. The presenters close by inviting the audience to Golden Gate B for the GraphRAG track, where they will reveal which of the ten memes are solved by graphs and graph technology.
